focus.text: A determiner is the small word that opens a noun phrase and tells your reader which one or how many: *a*, *the*, *this*, *my*, *most of*. English almost never leaves a singular countable noun bare, which is why *My father is doctor* stops a reader immediately. The choice between *a* and *the* comes down to one question: can the reader already tell which one you mean? Answer that question before you write the noun and most article problems disappear, because the rest of the phrase follows from it.

pretest.sentence: Mai's brother works as an engineer in Bình Dương.
pretest.reason: *Engineer* begins with a vowel sound, so *an* is right.

pretest.sentence: My aunt is teacher at a primary school in Huế.
pretest.reason: A singular count noun needs a determiner: *is **a** teacher*.

pretest.sentence: The library on our campus opens at seven.
pretest.reason: There is one library on the campus, so the reader knows which one.

pretest.sentence: The pollution is a serious problem in large cities.
pretest.reason: *Pollution* here means pollution in general, so it takes no article.

pretest.sentence: I borrowed a bicycle from a neighbour, and the bicycle had no lights.
pretest.reason: First mention takes *a*; the second mention takes *the*.

pretest.sentence: Government should spend more on public transport.
pretest.reason: *The government* is the one institution the reader already has in mind.

pretest.sentence: These photographs show how the river has changed.
pretest.reason: *Photographs* is plural, so the near demonstrative is *these*.

pretest.sentence: Sơn Đoòng is largest cave in the world.
pretest.reason: A superlative names the only one of its kind, so it takes *the largest*.

pretest.sentence: Most of students in my class travel by bus.
pretest.reason: After *of* the noun needs its own determiner: *most of **the** students*, or simply *most students*.

pretest.sentence: Each of the three groups presented a different solution.
pretest.reason: *Each of* is followed by *the* + a plural noun, and here it is.

context.title: The bookshop on the corner
context.paragraph: A small bookshop opened near our school last year, and the shop has changed how my friends spend their free time. The owner, Mr Quang, keeps a shelf of second-hand novels that cost less than a bowl of phở. Most of the students in my class now meet there on Friday afternoons. Books are still expensive in Vietnam, so a cheap shelf matters more than people expect. The quietest corner belongs to a reading club that Linh started in March, and the club already has thirty members. This habit has spread further: the school library reports that borrowing has almost doubled since the spring.

sections.title: Forming the noun phrase: a, an, the or nothing

table.caption: Which article goes in front of which noun

notes: *a* or *an* follows the **sound**, not the letter: **a** university, **a** European city, **a** one-way street, but **an** hour, **an** MA, **an** umbrella.
For a whole class of things, the plural with no article is the safest choice in essays: *Bicycles are cheap.* A singular (*A bicycle is cheap*) is also correct but sounds more like a definition.

items.reason: *Electrician* begins with a vowel sound, so use *an*.

items.stem: We watched a documentary about coral reefs. ___ film was made in Nha Trang.
items.reason: The film has already been mentioned, so the reader knows which one.

items.stem: ___ plastic waste is a growing problem on our beaches.
items.reason: A general uncountable noun takes no article.

items.stem: Huyền hopes to study at ___ university in Melbourne.
items.reason: *University* begins with a consonant sound, so use *a*.

items.stem: ___ sun was already low when we reached the pass.
items.reason: There is only one sun, so it takes *the*.

sections.title: Using a, an, the and no article

rules.text: Use *a* or *an* the first time you mention a singular countable thing, and when you say what somebody is.

examples.text: Her father is **an** electrician in Biên Hòa.

rules.text: Use *the* when the reader can already tell which one you mean, either because you have mentioned it or because there is only one.

examples.text: Our class visited a small museum. **The** museum was free for students.
**The** Mekong Delta produces most of the country's rice.

rules.text: Use no article with plural and uncountable nouns when you mean the thing in general.

examples.text: **Electric buses** are quieter than diesel ones.

tips: In IELTS Writing Task 2, general statements take no article: *Smartphones distract students.* Add *the* only when you narrow the group down: *the smartphones used in this survey*.

sections.title: Forming demonstratives and possessives

table.caption: Demonstratives and possessives, singular and plural

notes: A plural noun that already ends in -s takes only an apostrophe (*the students'*), but an irregular plural takes apostrophe + s (*the children's*).
*its* is the possessive (*the school and **its** library*); *it's* is short for *it is*. There is no apostrophe in the possessive.

items.stem: That laptop belongs to Khánh. It is ___ laptop.
items.reason: A singular owner takes apostrophe + s.

items.stem: ___ essays were all about the same film.
items.reason: A plural noun ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.

items.stem: ___ shoes over there are not mine.
items.reason: *Shoes* is plural and away from the speaker, so use *those*.

items.stem: Our school is proud of ___ new science lab.
items.reason: The possessive of *it* is *its*, written without an apostrophe.

items.stem: ___ two weeks have been the busiest of the term.
items.reason: *Weeks* is plural, so the near demonstrative is *these*.

sections.title: Using demonstratives and possessives

rules.text: Use *this* and *these* for what is near you or just mentioned, and *that* and *those* for what is further away in space or time.

examples.text: **This** report covers only the first six months.

rules.text: Match the demonstrative to the number of its noun: *this problem* but *these problems*.

examples.text: **These figures** come from a survey of 400 households.
**That kind** of mistake is easy to avoid.

rules.text: A possessive takes the place of *a* or *the*, so never use the two together.

examples.text: Nam left **his** bag on the bus.
**The city's** new metro line opened in August.

notes: Write *my teacher*, never *the my teacher*. Only one determiner can open a noun phrase.

sections.title: Using articles for general and unique reference, and quantifiers with of

rules.text: To write about a whole class of things, use a plural or uncountable noun with no article; adding *the* narrows it to a particular group.

examples.text: **Renewable energy** is cheaper than it was ten years ago.
**The renewable energy** used in this factory comes from solar panels.

rules.text: Use *the* with superlatives, ordinals and nouns that name the only one of something.

examples.text: Sơn Đoòng is **the largest** cave in the world.
**The first** paragraph should state your opinion.

rules.text: After a quantifier with *of* (*most of, some of, all of, none of, each of*), the noun needs its own determiner; without *of*, it does not.

examples.text: **Most of the students** in my class cycle to school.
**Most students** in Vietnam start English in primary school.

notes: Most city and country names take no article (*Huế*, *Vietnam*, *Japan*), but a few plural or descriptive names do (*the Philippines*, *the United Kingdom*, *the Mekong Delta*).
tips: *All of the* can drop its *of*: *all the students* and *all students* are both correct. But *most of students* is not English — keep *the* whenever *of* is there.

items.sentence: The unemployment is rising in several rural provinces.
items.reason: A general uncountable noun takes no article.

items.sentence: Government has promised to build two new hospitals.
items.reason: *The government* is the one institution the reader already has in mind.

items.sentence: My cousin wants to be a engineer like his mother.
items.reason: *Engineer* begins with a vowel sound, so the article is *an*.

items.sentence: Some of people in the survey had never taken a bus.
items.reason: Without a determiner after *of*, drop *of*: *some people*.

items.sentence: Huế is most peaceful city I have visited.
items.reason: A superlative names the only one of its kind, so it takes *the*.

editing.text: Last month our class took a trip to the Cần Thơ, where we spent two day studying life on the river. Our teacher, Ms Hương, arranged everything, and she is very patient guide. We left at five in the morning because traffic is terrible after six. At the floating market we watched a woman selling pineapples from a small boat, and she let us try one. Most of people there start work before dawn. A guide told us that government plans to widen the canal next year. In the afternoon we visited a rice mill and learned how the rice is dried. I took photographs of this machines for my geography project. These trip taught me more than a week of lessons, and I hope our school organises another one in June.

errors.reason: City names take no article, so write *Cần Thơ*.
A count noun after a number above one takes -s.
A singular count noun needs a determiner, so add *a*.
After *of* the noun needs its own determiner, so here drop *of*.
*The government* is the one the reader already has in mind, so it takes *the*.
*Rice* here means rice in general, and a general uncountable noun takes no article.
*Machines* is plural, so the demonstrative must be *these*.
*Trip* is singular, so the demonstrative must be *this*.

topics.prompt: Write an email to a friend in another city recommending one place in your town: a café, a park or a small shop. Say what it is, where it is and why you keep going back.
checklist: The first mention of each place uses *a* or *an*; later mentions use *the*.
General statements about food, prices or people use plural or uncountable nouns with no article.
Every singular countable noun has a determiner in front of it.

topics.prompt: Some people think city councils should make public transport free for students. Give your opinion and two reasons.
checklist: General statements use no article (*students*, *public transport*), not *the*.
*The* appears only where the reader can tell which one you mean (*the council in my city*).
At least one sentence uses a quantifier with *of* (*most of the students*, *none of the routes*).

topics.prompt: Describe your neighbourhood as it was five years ago and as it is today. Say what has stayed the same and what has changed.
checklist: Demonstratives match their nouns in number (*this street*, *these buildings*).
Possessives (*its*, *the street's*) replace the article instead of joining it.
Superlatives and unique nouns take *the* (*the busiest road*, *the only market*).
